objectives: Sequence the response steps after a credential is found in source control
Compare pre-commit, pre-receive, and CI secret scanning trade-offs
Explain why entropy-based and pattern-based detection produce different false-positive profiles
Choose the ggshield scan subcommand that fits a given workflow stage

questions.objective: Sequence the response steps after a credential is found in source control
questions.prompt: A live AWS access key was committed and pushed to a shared branch an hour ago. A teammate wants to start by purging the blob from git history. What should happen first?

options.text: Rewrite the branch history with git filter-repo so the blob disappears from the repo
Revoke and rotate the credential at its issuing provider before touching git history
Add the file to .gitignore and delete it in a follow-up commit on the branch
Force-push a revert of the offending commit and tell the team to re-clone
Leave the credential active until the git history rewrite proves that no copy remains

questions.explanation: Rewriting history does not invalidate the credential: forks, existing clones, CI caches, and provider APIs may still hold the blob, so the key keeps working for an attacker. History cleanup is worth doing, but it is cleanup, not containment.
questions.source: Lesson section: 'Step 5: Pair Detection with Response'

questions.objective: Compare pre-commit, pre-receive, and CI secret scanning trade-offs
questions.prompt: A platform team wants secret scanning that an individual developer cannot bypass. Which statements about the scanning stages are accurate?

options.text: A pre-commit hook runs on the developer's machine and can be skipped with git commit --no-verify
A pre-receive hook runs on the git server and can reject the push before the secret reaches the shared repo
A CI job sees the secret only after it has already been pushed to the remote
A GitGuardian pre-receive hook is impossible to bypass even when the server enables the documented breakglass push option
CI is the only stage able to inspect the full range of commits in a push

questions.explanation: Pre-commit runs locally and can be skipped, pre-receive runs on the VCS server and can reject a push, and CI normally scans after content reaches the remote. A pre-receive control is stronger than a local hook, but it is not inherently unbypassable: GitGuardian documents an optional `-o breakglass` push option when the server enables it.

questions.objective: Explain why entropy-based and pattern-based detection produce different false-positive profiles
questions.prompt: A scan flags a base64 test fixture and a UUID in a seed file, but misses an internal service token that looks like two ordinary words joined by a dash. What explains both results?

options.text: Pattern detectors match known provider prefixes, so they never flag encoded test data
The detector set lacked a rule for that token format and skipped the file entirely
High-entropy heuristics flag random-looking strings and miss low-entropy secrets
Entropy scoring applies only to files already in git history, not to the working tree
Entropy scoring applies only to provider-specific secrets whose prefix is already known

questions.explanation: Entropy heuristics trade precision for recall on unknown formats: anything random-looking scores high (false positives on fixtures and UUIDs) while a low-entropy homegrown token scores low. Option b describes the same miss but blames the wrong mechanism, since the file was scanned, just not matched.

questions.objective: Choose the ggshield scan subcommand that fits a given workflow stage
questions.prompt: Your CI job should scan only the commits included in the push that triggered the pipeline run. Which ggshield invocation does that?

options.text: ggshield secret scan path .
ggshield secret scan repo .
ggshield secret scan pre-commit
ggshield secret scan ci
ggshield secret scan archive .

questions.explanation: The ci subcommand reads the CI environment variables to work out the pushed commit range and scans exactly that. Option b would work but rescans the entire history on every run, which is slow and floods the job with pre-existing findings.

questions.objective: Sequence the response steps after a credential is found in source control
questions.prompt: A credential exposed in git history has been revoked and replaced. Which follow-up best completes the response?

options.text: Do nothing else because rotation guarantees that the committed value reveals no useful information
Delete the secret from the latest branch tip but leave history, caches, and artifacts unreviewed
Remove the secret from code and history where feasible, inspect copies in logs or artifacts, rescan, and document impact
Delete the entire repository so no incident record or audit evidence remains
Temporarily reactivate the old credential to test whether an attacker still has it

questions.explanation: Revocation is the immediate containment step, but cleanup and impact analysis still matter because the value and surrounding metadata may remain in clones, history, CI logs, and artifacts. OWASP explicitly says a leaked credential is compromised and should be invalidated, while the lesson adds history cleanup, rescanning, and prevention.

objectives: Choose between just-in-time and curriculum-style security learning for a given team problem
Assemble a finding-to-learning worksheet a developer can attach to a pull request
Explain why developer enablement is a required part of DevSecOps maturity
Pair a lesson concept with the tool that turns it into a repeatable control

questions.objective: Choose between just-in-time and curriculum-style security learning for a given team problem
questions.prompt: A dependency scan flags a prototype pollution CVE and the assigned developer does not understand the exploit path. How does this lesson say Snyk Learn should be used here?

options.text: Assign the complete OWASP Top 10 learning path before the fix is allowed to merge
Defer the topic to the next quarterly security training cycle for the team
Open the single lesson covering that vulnerability class while the finding is open
Suppress the finding until a formal security curriculum has been completed
Close the finding as accepted risk because training cannot change the vulnerable package

questions.explanation: The lesson's just-in-time model pairs a single module with a live finding, which is when retention is highest. Option a is the tempting one because a full path sounds more thorough, but it blocks the fix and separates the learning from the problem that motivated it.
questions.source: Lesson section: 'Step 5: Use it as a just-in-time learning tool'

questions.objective: Assemble a finding-to-learning worksheet a developer can attach to a pull request
questions.prompt: Which elements belong in the lesson's finding-to-learning remediation worksheet?

options.text: The affected package, endpoint, code path, or configuration
A recomputed CVSS environmental score for this deployment
A mapping to OWASP Top 10, CWE, or the closest lesson topic
One checklist item, test idea, or backlog task preventing recurrence
A signed security-team exception recorded before the fix merges

questions.explanation: The worksheet has to answer what is wrong, why it matters, how to fix it, and how the team avoids repeating it, so it needs the finding details, the class mapping, and a prevention action. A recomputed CVSS score is real work but not part of this artifact, and an exception is only needed when the team decides not to fix.

questions.objective: Explain why developer enablement is a required part of DevSecOps maturity
questions.prompt: A team already runs Trivy, Semgrep, and Checkov in CI, yet the same injection bug class reappears every sprint. Which gap does this lesson point to?

options.text: The severity thresholds on the pipeline gate are too permissive for that class
Findings are generated, but developers do not understand the class or the safe fix
The three scanners should be consolidated into one platform to cut duplicate noise
Runtime protection is required because static tooling cannot see injection bugs
The team has not uploaded its course-completion records to the compliance dashboard

questions.explanation: Recurrence after detection is an enablement problem, not a detection problem: the scanners are already flagging the class. Option a is plausible but a stricter gate would only block the same bugs later, without changing why developers keep writing them.

questions.objective: Pair a lesson concept with the tool that turns it into a repeatable control
questions.prompt: You have just finished a lesson on the risk of outdated container base images. Which follow-up does this lesson recommend to convert that knowledge into practice?

options.text: Run ZAP against the running container to confirm the packages are exploitable
Write a Checkov policy so Terraform rejects the base image at plan time
Scan the built image with Trivy and review the OS package findings
Re-read the OWASP DevSecOps Guideline compliance auditing chapter
Generate an SBOM but do not inspect the built image or its installed packages

questions.explanation: The lesson's pairing step maps image and dependency risk to Trivy, which inspects the built artifact's OS packages directly. ZAP is the tempting alternative, but a DAST proxy only sees HTTP behaviour and cannot enumerate what packages are installed in the image.
questions.source: Lesson section: 'Step 6: Pair education with implementation tools'

questions.objective: Explain why developer enablement is a required part of DevSecOps maturity
questions.prompt: Which evidence best shows that a team has closed a recurring secure-coding enablement gap?

options.text: Every developer opened the learning path at least once
The annual training dashboard reports a 100 percent completion rate
The security team increased the scanner severity without changing developer practice
Developers applied the fix pattern, added a regression check, and stopped reintroducing the weakness
The team archived the original findings without recording a prevention action

questions.explanation: Training attendance measures exposure, not comprehension or changed behavior. Applied remediation, a repeatable prevention control, and reduced recurrence demonstrate that developers can transfer the lesson into delivery work.
questions.source: Lesson sections: 'Step 4: Capture one remediation pattern from each lesson' and 'Key Takeaways'

objectives: Choose the correct Trivy subcommand and scanners for a given scan target
Configure Trivy to gate a CI build on severity and fix availability
Select a Trivy output format that matches the downstream consumer
Suppress a Trivy finding with .trivyignore and justify the exception

questions.objective: Choose the correct Trivy subcommand and scanners for a given scan target
questions.prompt: You need to check the Terraform in ./infra for security misconfigurations without building or pulling any image. Which command does that?

options.text: trivy config ./infra
trivy fs ./infra
trivy image --scanners misconfig ./infra
trivy repo --scanners vuln ./infra
trivy kubernetes ./infra

questions.explanation: trivy config is the dedicated misconfiguration subcommand for IaC directories. Plain trivy fs is the tempting choice, but misconfiguration detection is not enabled by default in the image, fs, and repo subcommands; you would have to add --scanners misconfig.

questions.objective: Configure Trivy to gate a CI build on severity and fix availability
questions.prompt: The build should fail only when there are CRITICAL vulnerabilities that already have a fixed version available. Which invocation implements that gate?

options.text: trivy image --severity CRITICAL --exit-code 1 app:latest
trivy image --severity CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 app:latest
trivy image --severity CRITICAL --ignore-unfixed app:latest
trivy image --severity CRITICAL --exit-code 0 --ignore-unfixed app:latest
trivy image --severity CRITICAL --format json app:latest

questions.explanation: --ignore-unfixed drops vulnerabilities with no available fix, and --exit-code 1 is what actually turns a finding into a failed job. Option c filters correctly but exits 0, so the pipeline reports findings and passes anyway.

questions.objective: Choose the correct Trivy subcommand and scanners for a given scan target
questions.prompt: Which statements about Trivy's --scanners option are correct?

options.text: vuln and secret are the default scanners for trivy image
Misconfiguration detection must be requested explicitly on image, fs, and repo
license is a valid scanner value alongside vuln, misconfig, and secret
--scanners sbom is how you produce a CycloneDX bill of materials
Enabling the secret scanner requires a paid Aqua subscription

questions.explanation: The four valid scanner values are vuln, misconfig, secret, and license, with vuln and secret on by default. SBOM output is not a scanner: it is a report format selected with --format cyclonedx or --format spdx-json.

questions.objective: Select a Trivy output format that matches the downstream consumer
questions.prompt: The team wants Trivy findings to land in GitHub's Security tab next to results from other scanners. Which --format value should the job emit?

options.text: json
cyclonedx
sarif
template
cyclonedx-json

questions.explanation: SARIF is the interchange format GitHub code scanning ingests, which is why the track's shared workflow uploads a .sarif file. JSON is machine-readable but GitHub will not render it as code scanning alerts.
questions.source: Lesson section: 'Step 5: Explore reporting and automation options'

questions.objective: Suppress a Trivy finding with .trivyignore and justify the exception
questions.prompt: A CRITICAL CVE in your base image has no fixed version upstream yet, and a release cannot wait. What is the most defensible way to unblock the pipeline?

options.text: Remove the --severity CRITICAL filter from the job so the finding stops being reported
Set --exit-code 0 on the scan step until the upstream maintainers ship a patch
Add --ignore-unfixed permanently so vulnerabilities without fixes never block
Add the CVE to .trivyignore with an exp: date, owner, and compensating control
Keep rescanning the unchanged image tag until the finding disappears from the database

questions.explanation: A .trivyignore entry scoped to one CVE with an exp:YYYY-MM-DD expiry keeps the gate intact for everything else and forces the exception back into review. Option c is the tempting one because this specific CVE has no fix, but it silently drops every unfixed finding forever, including future ones on internet-facing components.

objectives: Diagnose which pipeline gate was missing when a finding class reaches production
Place a security control at the correct delivery lifecycle phase
Assign ownership, evidence, and escalation to each control in a lifecycle map
Explain how the guideline treats tool choice and pipeline placement

questions.objective: Diagnose which pipeline gate was missing when a finding class reaches production
questions.prompt: A production incident traces back to a known CVE in a transitive npm dependency the team never imported directly. SAST and DAST both ran on every build and passed. Which control class was missing?

options.text: Software composition analysis resolving the full dependency tree
Container image scanning of the runtime base layer packages
Infrastructure-as-code policy checks ahead of the deploy step
Interactive application security testing in the staging tier
A secrets scan looking for credentials embedded in the npm lockfile

questions.explanation: Only SCA walks the lockfile and resolves indirect dependencies to known-vulnerable versions; SAST reasons about first-party source and DAST about runtime behaviour. Image scanning is the near miss: it would catch OS packages in the base layer, not a JavaScript package pulled in by another package.

questions.objective: Diagnose which pipeline gate was missing when a finding class reaches production
questions.prompt: A Terraform module created a production S3 bucket that was world-readable for two weeks. Application SAST, SCA, and container scanning all passed on every build. Which control would have caught this before deploy?

options.text: DAST run against the staging environment before promotion
Secrets detection on the pull request that added the module
Infrastructure-as-code policy scanning of the Terraform source
SBOM generation and signature verification at release time
Software composition analysis of the Terraform provider lock file

questions.explanation: The defect exists only in the infrastructure definition, so it is invisible to every control that looks at application code, dependencies, or image contents. DAST is the tempting answer, but a web scanner pointed at the app never exercises the bucket's ACL.
questions.source: Lesson section: 'Step 3: Build a control map by delivery phase'

questions.objective: Place a security control at the correct delivery lifecycle phase
questions.prompt: In the lesson's lifecycle control map, which phase-and-control pairings are correct?

options.text: Design - lightweight threat model owned by the feature team
Code - annual penetration test booked with an external assessor
Build - dependency, image, and IaC scans producing a SARIF artifact
Runtime - logging, alerting, and incident response owned by on-call
Deploy - line-by-line security review of every changed source file

questions.explanation: The map places fast, automated checks in code and build and reserves human judgement for design and runtime response. Options b and e are real activities but neither fits its phase: an annual pentest cannot gate individual commits, and manual review of every file cannot run at deploy cadence.

questions.objective: Assign ownership, evidence, and escalation to each control in a lifecycle map
questions.prompt: Your control map lists a build-time dependency scan with no named owner and no escalation path. What does the lesson identify as the practical consequence?

options.text: The scan silently stops running after the CI runner image is upgraded
Compliance frameworks automatically classify the pipeline as non-conformant
Findings get deduplicated incorrectly against the previous build's results
Findings accumulate with nobody accountable for triage or remediation
The scanner automatically suppresses every finding that lacks an owner field

questions.explanation: The guideline's point is that automation without ownership produces scan volume rather than risk reduction: the check runs, findings pile up, and no one is on the hook. The other options describe operational failures that ownership would not, by itself, cause or prevent.

questions.objective: Explain how the guideline treats tool choice and pipeline placement
questions.prompt: How should a team use the OWASP DevSecOps Guideline when choosing security tools and pipeline placement?

options.text: Adopt exactly one tool per activity at the single pipeline stage prescribed by OWASP
Select controls that fit the delivery lifecycle, place feedback as early as practical, and assign ownership and escalation
Replace all human review with scanners so every security decision is deterministic
Run every security activity only after production deployment to observe real behavior
Measure maturity by scanner count even when findings have no response owner

questions.explanation: OWASP describes security activities and a secure-pipeline model, but teams choose tools and locations appropriate to their lifecycle. The practical requirement is early useful feedback plus ownership, evidence, and response—not a fixed vendor toolchain or scanner count.
